speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: MR. CLAXTON  REFERENCE TO CORRESPONDENCE PUBLISHED IN "SATURDAY NIGHT"
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Yesterday the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) asked me a question about the conduct of the deputy minister of national defence, Mr. Drury. In view of the fact that other references have been made to that matter and that these all seem to be based upon a misapprehension, in fairness to the deputy minister, who cannot speak for himself here, I think I should make the matter more plain.

subtopic: MR. CLAXTON  REFERENCE TO CORRESPONDENCE PUBLISHED IN "SATURDAY NIGHT"
speechtext: His letter appeared in Saturday Night.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: MR. CLAXTON  REFERENCE TO CORRESPONDENCE PUBLISHED IN "SATURDAY NIGHT"
speechtext:
The letter to which reference was made was a letter from Mr. Drury addressed to Mr. Stevenson, not to Saturday Night; and it was Mr. Stevenson who chose to publish it. I might also draw attention to the fact that in the final paragraph of his letter of reply Mr. Stevenson said this:
I propose to ask the editor of Toronto Saturday Night to publish this correspondence between us.
That is the end of the paragraph and of the letter. That paragraph was not included in the edition of the reply published by Saturday Night or Mr. Stevenson, in the correspondence to which the hon. member referred.

subtopic: MR. CLAXTON  REFERENCE TO CORRESPONDENCE PUBLISHED IN "SATURDAY NIGHT"

speechtext: I should be glad to do so. I was waiting for the opportunity.

subtopic: MR. CLAXTON  REFERENCE TO CORRESPONDENCE PUBLISHED IN "SATURDAY NIGHT"
speechtext: I am waiting. Put both letters on the record.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: MR. CLAXTON  REFERENCE TO CORRESPONDENCE PUBLISHED IN "SATURDAY NIGHT"
speechtext: I think I should also read, from the article by Mr. Stevenson in Saturday Night of March 14, 1953, the passage to which Mr. Drury took exception quite properly because of the gross inaccuracy of the article.

Quite improperly.
68108-234J

In the sessions of the select committee on defence expenditures, the persistent efforts of its chairman, Mr. Croll, and his henchmen to smother damaging evidence of governmental waste and mismanagement has not availed to prevent the opposition members from unearthing some very damning material to sustain their case. They are now licking their chops over some candid reports by important officials-[DOT]
And I stress those words "important officials".
-and their severity can be gauged by the following two quotations:
"However, I could not fail to be impressed by the fact that for such a tremendous administrative machine there appears to be very little fighting strength", and "a high percentage of the construction and other contracts were awarded on a cost-plus basis, which the department itself has declared to be wasteful, inefficient, and an incentive to extravagance."

speakeroldname: Mr. G. J. Mcllraiih (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
On behalf of the minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) I should like to make a short statement.
Hon. members will have read or heard that the international wheat council, which has been meeting in Washington, has made recommendations to governments for a renewal of the wheat agreement. The following is the text of the press statement made yesterday by the chairman of the council:
The international wheat council decided by a substantial majority today to recommend to member governments that the international wheat agreement, which was due to expire on July 31 of this year, be extended for a further three-year period at a new price range of $2.05 maximum and $1.55 minimum to replace the present range of $1.80 maximum and $1.20 minimum.
The United Kingdom delegate informed the council, however, that while his government desired a renewal of the agreement it was not prepared to accept a maximum price above $2 per bushel.
Details with regard to the guaranteed imports and exports that would apply under the new agreement have not yet been decided. These will be announced as soon as this question has been settled.
In the course of the negotiations which began at the end of January, the council has also agreed to recommend to governments a number of textual amendments to be incorporated in the new agreement. These are being introduced largely on the basis of the experience gained in the operation of the wheat agreement since 1949 and are intended to clarify certain parts of the agreement and to improve its operation. None of these recommended changes, however, alter the basic principles on which the agreement was originally established.
A provision of the new agreement will permit the council, under certain conditions, to select an expert advisory panel to give the council an advisory opinion before taking a decision on any dispute arising on the application or interpretation of the agreement. The present position under which the council is the final arbiter on all disputes is unaffected.
Arrangements are being made for a formal signing ceremony which will be held within the next few days, after which the agreement will remain open for signature for a period of 14 days. Copies of the new agreement will be made available to the press at that time.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce is out of the city today. He will give a further explanation of the situation on Monday next.

In view of the fact that
the parliamentary assistant pointed out that the British representatives were not agreeable to that maximum, can he tell us what maximum price the British representatives were prepared to accept?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The statement I have
quoted-and this is the statement of the chairman of the council-contains this paragraph:
The United Kingdom delegate informed the council, however, that while his government desired a renewal of the agreement it was not prepared to accept a maximum price above $2 per bushel.
I might say that there will be a full statement on this subject by the minister on Monday.

speakeroldname: Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 228, to amend the Income Tax Act.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Robinson in the chair.
On section 1-Premium on redemption of shares.

Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to make more than a word of comment on the budget as such. I do however wish to make a few comments on the question of dominion-provincial-municipal tax problems.
As regards the budget itself, all I wish to say is that I think the public has been able to realize the truth of what I said in reply to the minister, that the minister has thought of everyone except the people; that 75 per cent of the people get little or no benefit from it; and that instead of his bringing in a social dividend, he brought in an antisocial dividend.
I wish now to turn to the question of dominion-provincial-municipal taxation problems. It is interesting to note that the great nation to the south of us is grappling with this problem in no uncertain way.
Income Tax Act
Their position, of course, in principle is very much the same as ours. The President has announced a project of inquiring into taxing and spending functions of the various taxing authorities. A commission is to be set up to stake out the proper areas for each authority. I should like to say in passing that that is what the Leader of the Opposition and other hon. members in the house have been asking repeatedly. It is also what the premier of Nova Scotia, Mr. Angus Macdonald, has been asking. And in this connection I would put on the record only a sentence from the Ottawa Journal of April 6 which, in commenting on this American proposal, says:
Why such a step has not been taken in Canada when its need is starkly imperative, all but passes understanding.
I would have liked it better if the words "all but" had been left out; because certainly I am unable to understand it. I can only imagine it is just another instance of that overholding power of people who have been in office for a long time, who lose touch, and who do not act in the way which ordinarily one would expect reasonable persons to act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not want to interrupt my hon. friend, because I am keenly interested in what he has to say. I think, however, that technically he is completely out of order in discussing on section 1, which amends certain sections of the Income Tax Act, such problems as federal-provincial-municipal taxing relations. If we were to proceed to discuss matters of that kind at this time, then frankly I do not know how any hon. member could be prevented from discussing any other matter which he might consider he wished to bring before the house.
I am sorry my hon. friend did not see Tit to make his comments in the course of the budget debate, or at some other time when, in doing so, he would have been within the rules of the house. I am in your hands, Mr. Chairman, of course; but I submit the hon. member is completely out of order in discussing this matter at the present time.

My understanding is that in the debate on section 1 of a bill we have been allowed considerable latitude. It seems to me this question is one of great practical importance, because it goes to the very root of taxation. As I have said, and now repeat, the range of discussion allowed on section 1 of a bill has been wide. If it will relieve the minds of hon. members at all, I might mention that I shall not be long in what I have to say.

Income Tax Act
I realize however that that does not go to the question of principle.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I quite agree with the hon. member for Greenwood when he says that we have allowed a wide range of discussion on clause 1 of a bill. But I would point out that that range is limited to the principle of the bill itself. I would ask the hon. member to confine himself to general remarks on the principle of the bill which, in this instance, is an act to amend the Income Tax Act.

With deference, Mr. Chairman, I submit that, among other things, this is a bill to raise money. I do submit that questions affecting the dominion's need for revenue, which I am trying to discuss when I open up this whole question of the distribution of responsibilities between the dominion and the provinces, is within the scope of the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I must differ with my hon. friend. I have a keen interest in his views, and I am sure they would be well worth listening to. But if we do not adhere to the rules of the house, then I just do not see how we can have any sort of orderly debate.
The question my hon. friend is raising is a very important one. I dealt with it at length in my budget speech. In his reply my hon. friend did not deal with it at any great length. But I suggest that was the time to deal with this general question of the financial relationships between different levels of government in Canada, and that it is not properly debatable when section 1 of a bill to amend the Income Tax Act is called.

Mr. Chairman, while the
minister may have no intention of curtailing debate in the matter, it seems to me the income tax is so closely related to and interwoven with the question of dominion-provincial relations that it might properly be discussed at this time. The income tax is one of the major tax fields, and it has been under discussion many times in dominion-provincial discussions.
It seems to me that, on that basis, the hon. member is not asking too much when he asks for the opportunity to finish his remarks on this point. I suggest that he be given that opportunity. It may be that Mr. Chairman may wish to give a ruling on the point. I am sure however that the hon. member for Greenwood is not one who makes it a habit to encroach upon the rules of the house, for any purposes whatsoever. I suggest that he be given the opportunity to finish his remarks.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I am sure hon.
members will realize that I have no wish to curtail debate in any way. But as has been pointed out by the Minister of Finance, under our rules there are proper occasions upon which the debate on certain subjects should take place.
I must agree with the point of order taken by the Minister of Finance when he says that the remarks of the hon. member for Greenwood are too broad in scope. I would therefore ask the hon. member to co-operate by adhering in his remarks to the principle of the bill before us.

Well, Mr. Chairman, that was the one subject I wished to talk about. If that is ruled out of order, the committee will not have the pleasure of hearing me at all.
I suggest, with deference, that my whole understanding has been that when section 1 of a bill has been called there has been a wide-open opportunity for discussion. It seems to me that when the minister suggests this matter was discussed by him in his budget speech, and that then, and then only, was the time to discuss the matter further-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not necessarily the only time.

I say that
when the minister suggests that this is not the proper time, his interpretation is too narrow. However, if that is your ruling, Mr. Chairman, I shall have to defer to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As I say, I am always anxious to hear what my hon. friend has to say. I think however that there may be another opportunity for him to speak on this subject when my estimates are under consideration. I think there are some items in the estimates of the Department of Finance which should afford him the opportunity to make the observations he wishes to make-but not today.

As an experienced legislator in this chamber, the minister knows that the practical result, when debate is curtailed as it is now suggested it should be, is that it breaks out on a motion to go into supply. If we are going to get this house closed in reasonable time early in May I should think the minister will have to take a different course than to suggest to the chairman that this be not proceeded with. I think that will only add to confusion in the end. I can only hope that the hon. member will be allowed to finish.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I wonder if I might offer a
suggestion. This problem comes up often, and I recognize the validity of the point which the Minister of Finance seeks to make. This is a bill amending an existing statute. I think the confusion arises by reason of the fact that sometimes bills that come before us are brand new. When that happens it is the usual practice that a general discussion is allowed on section 1, which is usually the short title. But when we get a bill amending an existing statute, such as this bill, section 1 usually amends some section down the line in the statute and that right of general discussion is not usually extended. I think that that is the reason for the confusion.
However, it does seem to me that the remarks which the hon. member for Greenwood was trying to make would have been in order on the second reading of this bill while Mr. Speaker was in the chair. If that is correct, it might therefore be argued that the same remarks would be in order on third reading. I offer that as a suggestion. If it is not acceptable to have this speech made now the hon. member might be allowed to make it on third reading.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If it is within the rules I
would not have the slightest objection.

The trouble with me is that I am too co-operative and I did not stand up while Mr. Speaker was in the chair because I thought that that might slow up matters. I am not going to press the matter further. I was going to make the suggestion which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has been good enough to make, and perhaps I shall deliver my remarks on the third reading of the bill.

I should like to ask the
minister one or two questions on the first section. The other day we had a discussion with regard to allowing the cost of reforestation as an operating expense. It will be found in Hansard of March 20. The Minister of Resources and Development entered into the discussion and said in effect that there had been some arrangement made within the last few weeks whereby these expenses would be allowed. On further questioning he admitted, as will be found on page 3149 of Hansard, that this allowance would be made only where the taxpayer had what is known, in British Columbia at least, as a forest management licence. I would ask the minister to explain just what this new provision covers. There are comparatively few firms which hold forest management licences. Practically all of them are quite large concerns and I am worried whether
Income Tax Act
this provision will be applicable to the small operator who does not hold a forest management licence.
My other question has to do with the possibility of obtaining an exemption to cover the costs of nursery and child care incurred by a mother who is working. The minister will remember I dealt with that in my budget speech. I would ask him to let us know whether any consideration has been given to my request and if there is any possibility of obtaining that exemption.
My third question has to do with out-oftown travelling and living expenses of persons engaged in the building and construction trades. This matter also was raised during the budget debate and I should like to know what stand the government is taking.
Finally I should like to know what changes are being made with regard to pension funds. The minister stated during the budget debate, and I quote from page 2129 of Hansard as follows:
Special provision will be made to alleviate the tax on refunds paid out as a result of reorganizations of pension plans. This will apply, of course, in the case of the Canadian National Railways pension plan reorganization which has been of interest to many hon. members.
Complaints have been made that because this reorganization plan will mean the payment of lump sums to the recipients the Department of National Revenue is taking the position that the whole payment will be taxable in the year in which it is received. That seems to be a most unfair arrangement and I would ask the minister to explain in what manner the problem is being dealt with by this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall answer the last question first. It is dealt with in a section a little later in the bill, but in essence the payment which is being made as a result of the reorganization of the Canadian National pension fund will result, as I understand it, in quite substantial lump sum payments being made to pensioners.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Are we on section 12?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is taking exception.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister suggested that we should follow the rules.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra was completely put of order with the questions he asked on section 1, but I thought that as the questions related directly to the Income Tax Act perhaps it would not be stretching the rules too far to answer them at this time. Every one of the questions he asked

Income Tax Act
was out of order under section 1. I am quite willing to give information on this section as I think perhaps that would be within the spirit of a discussion on section 1. What I objected to strongly was discussing general philosophic principles on section 1 of the bill. If the committee wants to adhere strictly to the rules, needless to say I will be delighted to do so.
It is a pretty well established practice that there is wide discussion permitted on section 1 of a bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I could answer that question when we deal with section 12 which relates directly to the Canadian National pension plan. I will give this information when we reach that section because some other hon. members may have questions to ask.
As to this matter of the cost of reforestation, I am not exactly clear as to what my colleague may have been referring to as I was not in the house at the time. I am informed that it is a question of fact in each case. If the expense incurred by the taxpayer is an operating expense, if it can be considered as an operating expense, it is deductible. On the other hand, if it is of a capital nature then it is a capital charge and would be subject to capital cost allowances and written off over a period of years.
Then the hon. member asked about the cost of nursing. I understand he is referring to the practical nurse who might be brought in to look after children while the mother is out working. There again we have never felt that under the Income Tax Act we can allow deductions from salaries and wages as expenses. Salaries and wages, with certain exceptions with which my hon. friends are familiar, are considered as income. It is difficult, if not impossible, to draw a line between what expenses might be allowed and what expenses cannot be allowed. While this arouses a good deal of sympathy it is not a matter on which we feel we could breach the important principle which is involved.
Then the third point was the expenses of construction workers on out of town jobs. I must say that we gave that matter a tremendous amount of anxious consideration because I realize that these days, with active construction programs going on in a great many parts of the country, it is necessary for construction workers to move from one part of the country to another and in doing so maintain their permanent homes wherever they may happen to be resident. But here again, on this basic principle to which we have adhered, salaries and wages are taxable

income by definition and the taxpayer is not entitled to deduct living expenses. He can, in the circumstances set out in the act, deduct expenses when he is in travel status as defined in the act, but unfortunately in a good many instances that does not meet the cases to which my hon. friend refers.
All I can say is that, after a great deal of careful consideration and discussion with my officials and the officials of the Department of National Revenue, we felt we could not make this further exception in the law. I had discussions on the matter with representatives of the trade unions who put their case before me very fully and fairly. I should have liked to be able to grant it but it just was not possible.

Are there not other groups who are already getting that exemption? Their travelling and living expenses are being allowed, and I think that the men in the construction trades could be brought in under the same category, or perhaps it would require an amendment to the act. Then there is the further fact that the consxruction industry is of vital importance to Canada today, and I know that it is becoming difficult in British Columbia to get men to go to projects in the more remote parts of the province. I believe there is some danger that developments which would otherwise take place may be held back because this exemption is not allowed. The question came up there in this form. The unions actually entered into an agreement with management under which these costs would be paid by the employers, but then they were taxed so that the agreement did not help at all. I think this merits a further check by the Department of Finance and the Department of National Revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The union agreements to which my hon. friend referred were not exactly on the basis he outlined. What happened under the union agreements was that it was provided that the worker would be paid a certain sum of money in lieu of travelling and living expenses. It is perfectly open to the employer to reimburse his workers for their actual out of pocket travelling and living expenses, but apparently that involves some added expense and difficulty, and as you know we have a very strict rule against lump sum expense allowances. Consequently we did not feel that an addition to the per diem or per hourly rate to compensate for out of pocket expenses could be allowed. I realize that is a simple and perhaps efficient way of handling it, but nevertheless it does breach the principle to which I have alluded.

With respect to the second point, deduction of the cost of nursery and child

care in the case of a mother who is working, would the mother not be in a similar position to a professional man who hires a stenographer to help him earn his income?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, because he is on a gross basis. He gets fees and he charges his expenses before he arrives at his net. He is not being paid a salary. She is being paid a salary.
The reason she cannot get the exemption is that she is getting a salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is a fundamental distinction in our law. As my hon. friend knows,
I have explained before that salary and wages, by definition, are income. If a man is an independent contractor or a professional man he grosses up his fees, deducts his office rent, salaries, stationery and other expenses and arrives at his net. That is his taxable income. But if he is hired by a corporation for a salary, then presumably the corporation pays those expenses and charges them up as an expense of doing business. For instance, as I pointed out, a man who is a salaried employee cannot get a deduction for the expenses of a maid to look after his children. It is a fundamental principle.
That is a different situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Nor could a professional man.
Suppose the mother is carrying on a business of her own such as running a public stenographer's office. Could she then deduct these costs?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. She could deduct the expenses of running her office but she could not deduct any of her home expenses.

If the minister will investigate the situation further, I think he will find that the working mother is at an unfair disadvantage in so far as these exemptions are concerned. I hope that further consideration will be given to the matter. With respect to the allowance for reforestation, the minister has not yet made it clear to me at least in what manner that applies. Will these tax deductions be applicable to any legitimate forest operation in which the taxpayer is working on a sustained yield unit program?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As my hon. friend knows, the dividing line between what is a capital expenditure and an operating expense is sometimes very hard to draw. Take this case as an example. Suppose by virtue of one of these management licences, or whatever the correct description is, there is taken over a tract of land that has already been cut over and puts into effect a large-scale reforestation program. What is then being done in effect is to create a new capital asset. That would be a capital expenditure and as the timber was cut depletion depreciation could be taken.
Income Tax Act
But the timber would not be cut for many years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is quite true. It is the same way when you build a plant. The plant is amortized over a long period of time. On the other hand, in the case of a current operation, where as the operator cuts down some trees he plants new ones as a part of his general operation, my information is that the wages and salaries in that operation can be considered as operating expenses. But as I say, it is very difficult to lay down a hard and fast rule as to what in a given case is capital and what is an operating expense. Almost every case has to be looked at on the facts of the particular case.

Perhaps the minister can deal with it in this way. Will this new arrangement, which apparently was made in February of this year, be applicable to only a handful of the very large operators who have forest management licences from the provincial government of British Columbia or will it be applicable to the forest industry as a whole?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that it applies from coast to coast.

How will it work out in British Columbia? Will it only apply to the dozen or so who have forest management licences or will it apply to the hundreds of smaller men who are carrying on forest operations and in many cases are doing reforestation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told it applies to them all.
If that is right that is satisfactory.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is my information. The same rule applies to all.
My understanding is that so far the smaller men do not know anything about it. They were quite surprised to hear that an arrangement had been made, and presumably it was made with the big operators.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed by the deputy minister of national revenue that it applies to all of them. There is no distinction between the two groups.

I should like to ask a question or two. The first matter is one on which I have a great deal of difficulty in defending the government when I am in my own constituency, and you can readily realize that is a problem I should like to have solved here. Also people keep asking me why it is that when the wife dies the husband then must go into another status from the point of view of income tax. He cannot any longer claim marital status as a householder operating a self-contained establishment. In most of these instances where they come to me, and

Income Tax Act
where I have to put up as good a case for the government as I can, I find it very difficult to defend that position. That is, of course, not the only instance where I have trouble defending the government but it is true in this case particularly.
In most instances the man of the house has greater expenses by virtue of the change in status than he did before. It may be that something has been done in connection with this legislation and if so I would personally welcome it and ask the minister if he has given consideration to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As the hon. member knows, a widower, or even an unmarried man, who is maintaining a self-contained domestic establishment and supporting someone in it who is dependent on him for support, is entitled to the marital exemption.
Yes, but that is not the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A widower who has no children and is not supporting anyone and who prefers to live in his house instead of living at a club does not get the $2,000 exemption. He is treated as a single person. A widower who supports children and who lives in a home continues to get the $2,000 exemption.

The problem arises where the widower has children in the home who are perhaps over the age limit. Those are the cases with which I am having difficulty because people cannot see the reasoning. I must confess too that I cannot see why that exemption cannot be allowed to a widow or a widower as the case may be.
I know that you cannot extend this all over the place and allow it to run wild as far as these self-contained establishments are concerned, but surely there must be some definition that can be drawn without getting into administrative difficulty or meeting administrative obstacles which are too great to hurdle. I would like the minister to give some further consideration to the matter because it does seem to me that there are instances where the government might go some distance without infringing too far upon their administrative regulations.
The other point I want to mention is one I raised last year. I know that the minister must have given some consideration to this and it arises out of little people being in business-people who employ perhaps one or two others and who are just managing to get by. These people are finding that they must work for nothing in the collection of these income tax payments, and I do not think that the little fellow particularly ought to carry the government's load without in some way receiving remuneration for it.

I can understand that perhaps this does not mean so much to those who have a big set-up where they can deduct the cost of doing these things; but I could never understand why the government needs to be hitchhiking on top of the little fellow as far as the expense of these collections is concerned. The government has money for other things and it seems to me that the situation is pretty intolerable from the little man's point of view.
I raised this matter last year and I coupled with it the statement that if all of the members of the house were to go into some little business and see just what they would have to do for this government, without getting a five-cent piece in return, they would be astounded. They would have to collect unemployment insurance; they would have to collect these income tax payments; and by the time they got around to answering all the questions asked by the dominion bureau of statistics they would find that they did not have time to look after their own business. I do not think that situation should be tolerated or continued. The minister I think said that it was an instance of good citizenship. Well, you can extend good citizenship pretty far-to the point where citizens are out of business. It is pretty difficult for me to see why some leniency might not be shown at least to some people in the way of relieving them of carrying further burden. I know the minister will have an answer, and it will be one of those answers which have been carefully gone over by the administrative staff. Nevertheless, I think there is a case where at least somebody ought to champion the little fellow who is making so many of these deductions and who is carrying so much of this load. It is pretty difficult to make ends meet in little business today; and I think that what you are doing in many instances is driving little business into the hands of big business.
Hear, hear.

I confess that the difficulty I mention does not apply so much to big business and I am, of course, only talking about the little fellow. He is entitled to be given a little break on this, whether you give him the break in some compensatory way here or on something else.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I told my hon. friend last year, when he raised this question, I share his solicitude for the little fellow; but it does not require any high-priced help to give one answer to this problem. This income tax deducted at the source, and unemployment insurance deductions, must be collected by somebody. If the employer does not do it we will have to hire a few thousand more civil

servants, pay them to do it, and then tax the little fellow among others to pay for that service.
My own belief is that the present system whereby the taxpayer makes the deductions and remits them is about as efficient and cheap a way of doing the job as there is. Under those circumstances I think he makes his contributions through the services of himself or staff rather than as a taxpayer. If he has a bookkeeper he can charge up the expense of the bookkeeper as an expense of doing business. I think that successive governments, this one and those preceding it, have found that this system is about as fair a way of collecting these payments as can be found.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I wonder if I might ask the minister a question on clause 1.
Hear, hear.
Ask it on third reading.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I realize that I am being extraordinary in dealing with the matter before the house.
I have two questions that I would ask. First, will the minister explain why he is bringing in this clause at all? What was wrong with the taxing of premiums received on the acquisition of shares?
My second question is this: Why is a section like this being made retroactive when some other sections such as those dealing with the allowances for children attending university or the change in the level at which medical expenses are allowed, are not being made retroactive?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will deal with the last question first.
In the amendment to the act in 1949, provision was inserted providing for tax on acquisition of shares at a premium. I do not believe that there was very widespread general knowledge of that amendment which introduced the word "acquisition". What happened was that in the case of a number of companies which proposed to redeem their shares at a premium-and in some cases at a substantial premium-they did it by purchasing shares on the market. A man would buy shares of this company, hold them perhaps a month or two and sell them, not realizing that he was selling to a person who was in fact buying them for redemption by the company. I had some instances brought to my attention where a tax liability of say $10,000 or $12,000 was created where in fact the purchaser and seller of the shares had suffered a small loss on the transaction.
It was quite easy, for anyone who knew the ropes, and who knew those shares were
Income Tax Act
being redeemed, to legally avoid the payment of any such tax. The shares are being either acquired by or held by a Canadian tax-exempt organization and as such the tax would not apply. So it seems to me that there was a trap in the law which should not be continued; and it led to an examination of the whole question of the taxation of the premiums on the redemption of shares. It seemed desirable to make a fundamental change and to provide as the law now does, or as the law will provide if this bill is passed, that in the case of redemption of shares at a premium, the premium may be paid out of tax-paid undistributed income if the company is one which has created such a form of tax-paid income. If not, there will be a special tax of 20 per cent of the premium imposed upon the redemption of those shares.
This is fairly technical, I know, but I think it is a satisfactory solution to a problem which, I may say quite frankly, has bothered me for a long time. As I say, anybody who knew the ropes could always avoid the payment of taxes on shares being redeemed at a premium and it was only the people who either did not know how to go about it or who did not know that the redemption was going to take place, who got caught. In this way we will be sure of getting a reasonable tax on the premium on the redemption of shares.
The 20 per cent rate is 5 per cent in excess of the rate at which, it will be recalled, pre-1949 surpluses can be capitalized as tax-paid undistributed income. The committee will also recall that as to profits since that time, if half are paid out as dividends, the other half may be created into a tax-paid surplus. That is the general basis on which this amendment to the law is made. There are two or three other sections relating to it.

In the light of the explanation which he has just given, may I ask the minister whether it is likely to mean the opening up of a good many returns in the case of taxpayers who have already been taxed on the premiums they received on the redemption of shares?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think there will unquestionably be reopening of some returns because there were really some hard cases brought to my attention. I was shocked at the inequity of some of them and that is what really prompted the introduction of this measure. I think it will involve the reopening of some of the returns. A number of appeals were taken which I think are still pending. The assessments will be revised. It is pointed out that there will be a reassessment of these

Income Tax Act
returns by the department and a revised notice of assessment will be issued.

In all these cases will the department take the responsibility in connection with the reassessment? No doubt the period has passed for entering an appeal against those assessments going back to 1949 income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told it all arose as a result of the reassessment by the department. They picked this up in the returns. I think there are perhaps not a large number of securities involved because there have been a limited number of companies who, during the last two or three years, have acquired shares for redemption.

I should like to be clear on this. In the case of a taxpayer whose assessment was made, let us say, on 1949 or 1950 income, where the file is closed and the usual period for entering any appeal against the assessment is past, do I understand that the department will in that case take the responsibility for reopening the assessment and making the refund for any excess paid, in the light of this retroactive legislation. There is not much use of our passing legislation intended to be retroactive for the relief of a taxpayer if the period for reopening his assessment has passed and the time for appeal is past, unless the department is prepared to take responsibility for reopening the assessment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As my hon. friend will recall, it applies only to the case of the acquisition of shares, not to redemptions. I think the onus must be on the taxpayer. If the assessment has been made and the time for appeal has expired and no appeal was lodged and the tax was paid, it is up to him to make application for reopening and refund; and that would be given to him.
Even though his period for appeal has passed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, quite.
The department will allow that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, yes. Everybody will be treated equally.

Mr. Chairman, I presume that everyone is presumed to know what the law is but in fact not everybody does. Is it sufficient for the department merely to say that it will not invoke the passage of time for appeal? Is it asking too much that the department will, as I understand the hon. member for Eglinton to say, assume responsibility for reassessment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The department will, I think, reassess; but I think the onus must remain on the taxpayer of asking to have the assessment reopened and of claiming a refund of the tax which he has paid.

He may not
know about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think most of them know it. My impression is that a great many of them know about it.

I gather that this measure refers only to preferred stocks which were redeemed by operations in the open market. It does not apply to preferred stocks which were redeemed at a premium, shall we say, of five points over par?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It does not apply to those retroactively; but it does apply retroactively to preferred shares which were acquired in the open market by the company. But as my hon. friend knows and as the committee know, these shares would be bought in the market in the ordinary way. The vendor would not have any idea to whom he was selling. He might think he was selling to another investor when in fact the purchase was being made by the company. It is that type of case that we are providing the relief for. For the future we have a new system for handling the redemption of preferred shares with this special tax of 20 per cent unless it is paid out of tax-paid undistributed income. But the retroactive relieving part applies only to what I might describe as the cases of the innocent bystanders who did not realize that they were involving themselves in any tax liability.
It refers clearly to the monetary premium?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

It does not refer, for instance -although I do not know that there were any of these cases-to a preferred stock which was redeemable in terms of common stock or transferable in terms of common stock and the aggregate of the common stock conversion was higher than the selling price of the preferred stock?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It does not apply to redemption at all in the past; purely to acquisition.

Mr. Chairman, I have one question to ask. I am afraid that it is a little bit out of order but I can see no other section under which I can ask it. The minister has been wandering a little bit in answering some of the other questions and I wonder if he will answer this one. Can the

principle of employee deductions be extended to employees of the American bases? I have been requested to ask whether arrangements could be made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall have to look into this matter. We would be happy to do it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 2-Municipal officers expense allowance.

This is the clause which refers to the expense allowance of municipal officers. We had quite a lengthy debate on the resolution dealing with this matter. At that time there was some question as to whether an elected officer would include a member of a school board and of a parks board. Can the minister tell us whether this amendment is meant to cover those officers or only persons elected to council?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not intended to cover school boards. It is intended to cover only elected municipal officers and to extend to them the same principle that applies to us as members of parliament or to members of provincial legislatures. There is nothing, of course, to prevent members of school boards from being paid their out of pocket expenses, on an actual basis; that is, being reimbursed the actual out of pocket expenses which they incur as members of the school board. There is not, and there never has been, anything to prevent a municipal officer from being reimbursed his actual out of pocket expenses incurred in the performance of his municipal duties. But, as we know, that involves a considerable amount of keeping track of expenses and so on. Since we ourselves here as elected representatives provided a lumpsum allowance for expenses which it is well recognized we have to incur, it seemed desirable and appropriate to extend that same privilege to the principal elected officials of other bodies. This is for the municipalities. My information is-and it is certainly true in my own province-that very few members of school boards receive anything in the way of remuneration. It should be borne in mind that one can only get this expense allowance if one is voted specifically and it must not exceed one-third of the combined total. But there is nothing to prevent any of these other officials being reimbursed for their actual out of pocket expenses.

The wording of the new clause is:
Where an elected officer of an incorporated municipality has been paid . . .
It does seem to me that a member of a school board is an elected officer, as is a member of a parks board. I do not see why
Income Tax Act
they should not get the same treatment. As a matter of fact, when the resolution was before the committee I argued that they should be treated in the same way as the members of the council. I believe that the way the section is worded it is wide enough to cover them. The minister now says they are not going to be covered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They were not intended to be covered. It may be that the section is wide enough to cover them. I do not think it is, personally, but we certainly did not intend to cover them. This is a new departure and I would certainly not recommend extending it beyond the elected municipal officials. None of the school board officers need be out of pocket. They can get their actual expenses. I do not think many of them are paid remuneration. I served on a school board once; I did not get remuneration for doing it; I do not think most people do. This is a new departure. It is the sort of thing we will look at another year, but it does represent a very substantial concession to municipal officials. Mark you, they have to be voted remuneration plus expenses. They cannot be voted just a lump sum for expenses; it must be a combined sum, and the expense portion of the sum must be not in excess of one-third of the total.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In some provinces of the country, and particularly in the west, school board members are elected officials. In my own city, for example, they are just as much elected officials as are the members of council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are in a lot of other places.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And they are paid remuneration for their services. I will not argue the merits or demerits of the general principle of the exemption, but it does seem to me that the two groups should be treated on the same basis.

I should like to ask the minister a question on this because I took the trouble to send copies of Hansard to a large number of municipal officers in my own constituency, and I know there was a great deal of confusion in their minds as to the real meaning of this. The intent is clear, that it is desirable that elected municipal officers who receive an expense allowance for which-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not go that far. This is purely enabling legislation. I do not think it is desirable.

It is enabling legislation. In order to benefit from this legislation, does the municipality have to pass a minute of council or a specific bylaw stating that the

Income Tax Act
salary shall be so much and the expense shall be half of the salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right, not more than half the salary.
Not more than half.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Appropriate municipal action must be taken.

The point in connection with this very attractive looking section is that it is not going to operate fairly among all municipalities, and I am going to point out the significant words. A moment ago the minister admitted with frankness that before anyone could qualify in respect of the retroactive effect of this section it would be necessary for that person to be voted a sum to include remuneration plus expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

And that is the significance of this section. That is the point I intend to raise in connection with it because it is not going to be fairly applied everywhere across this country. The section reads as follows:
Where an elected officer of an incorporated municipality has been paid by the municipal corporation an amount as an allowance in a taxation year for expenses incident to the discharge of his duties as an elected officer of the corporation, the allowance shall not be included in computing his income for the year unless it exceeds one-half of the amount that was paid to him in the year . . .
The significant words there are: "has been paid", and a little later on, "was paid". Take the situation in some provinces of this country. There is no provision in the legislation of those provinces for an honorarium to include expenses. Take my own province; take the province of Ontario. These provinces have legislation that permits the payment of honoraria, and have had that legislation over the years, but that legislation does not include any provision for expenses as part of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Ontario has now amended its statute.

I am going to come to that. The interpretation placed on that legislation of Ontario already by some of the officials is that it is not effective. At the current session of the Ontario legislature legislation was passed, and I will come back to that in a moment.
As I understand it, with very few exceptions, there are at the present time but one or two municipalities to which the retroactive feature of this legislation will apply. One is the city of Montreal-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

The city of Montreal has its own legislation to the effect that an amount is paid as an honorarium which is to include in addition an allowance for expenses. Other municipalities have not that legislation, and the result is going to be that in so far as the retroactive effect of this legislation is concerned the only ones who would benefit from it are the members of the municipality of Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think there is one other, or there may be one or two others. There may be quite a few; I do not know.
Will the minister tell us who the others are?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot remember them-the city of Quebec.
I did not know that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know about the other provinces.
All right; the city of Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not familiar with the others.

This is a very good principle. The city of Montreal and the city of Quebec, which was mentioned by the parliamentary assistant, have this legislation. I did not know that, but they have adopted a very farseeing piece of legislation in making that provision. Others have not done that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They will now.

Oh, yes. I am speaking about the retroactive effect. That is the important thing here. Others, not having adopted it, are placed in a position where no municipality other than the one or two that have been mentioned particularly will benefit from this retroactively. I think no one wants to bring in legislation that is going to deny municipal officials all the way across Canada the same equality in its retroactive effect.
A while ago the minister said that Ontario has this legislation. At the current session provision was made for a division of the amount to be paid to elected municipal officials. In addition, within that legislation provision was made that the division should be considered to have been retroactive in effect. The amendment states that one-third of .the salary back to 1946 shall have been deemed to have been paid for expenses. When the minister says that that legislation has been passed, that is true. It was passed at the recent session. But according to the officials administering this legislation, the provision is unacceptable to the authorities administering the income tax. While I do

not have them on my desk at the moment, I have seen documents from the treasury branch stating that it is unacceptable.
The amendment will not be fair and reasonable unless the departmental officials administering it will agree that it shall apply wherever a province passes an amendment to its municipal act, and makes in that act a provision whereby whatever honoraria have been paid shall be considered to have been two-thirds honoraria and one-third expenses. Otherwise an injustice will be done to elected municipal officials, everywhere in Canada, with the exception of two or three urban municipalities.
Municipal officials are a group of public servants who, too often, must shoulder the responsibilities of public office, and have but little of the appealing side enjoyed by members of parliament and of legislatures. There are many people who think there are no compensations in public life. The minister would not be here if there were not. There is the satisfaction in the service performed, and in all parts of the house men are giving their services unselfishly and in a spirit of personal sacrifice, knowing that the monetary returns are not great.
From now on, however, municipal officials are to be extended equality with members of the dominion parliament and of provincial legislatures. However, if the retroactive effect of the legislation is to apply only in the case of two municipalities which, in their foresight, made provision some years ago for an actual division as between honoraria and expenses, then I say the section should be amended so as to allow all municipal officials who have received honoraria since 1946 to be placed in the same position as the officials in those two municipalities. There may be more, but the minister mentioned two of them. While I have no knowledge of them, there may be others.
Certainly an appeal to the minister to make a provision to give equality everywhere is not an appeal to special interests. It is not an appeal for any particular individuals. Rather, it is an appeal that municipal officials everywhere in our country shall be treated with equality under this legislation.
The Ontario legislature decided to meet the situation and, as I said, passed legislation at the present session. However, up until the eighth day of April the authorities had not notified the government of Ontario, or the treasury officials of that province, that the amendment would be acceptable in so far as those municipal officials are concerned.
I should like to ask the minister to elucidate the situation. I noticed that he was at great pains to accentuate the situation where the
Income Tax Act
vote that had been made heretofore, and prior to the coming into effect of this legislation, covered remuneration plus expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In answer to my hon. friend I would say only this, that this matter was carefully considered and it was decided to make the section retroactive so as to apply to cases where, in fact, the appropriation or allocation of remuneration and expenses had been segregated, and that we were not going to make it retroactive to other cases.

That is exactly the point I have made, and the minister supports it. My interpretation of the effect of this section is correct. Now I ask him this question: Legislation was passed by the legislature of Ontario, in its recent session, and in which I believe provision has been made that it shall be considered that since 1946 the amount paid for honoraria to municipal elected officials shall be deemed to be divisible by two-thirds as honoraria and one-third as expenses. Is the minister prepared to say that that legislation will be recognized by his department, and that all municipal officials will be retroactively considered for income tax purposes to have received the amount provided for expenses in the legislation passed by the Ontario legislature? If so, I have no doubt similar legislation will be passed by the legislatures of other provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have before me a copy of the bill passed in the Ontario legislature, adding a section to the municipal act. It is an enabling section. I do not think I shall take the time to read it. However, it does permit municipal corporations, by an appropriate bylaw or resolution, to provide that one-third of the total remuneration, not to exceed $2,000, may be deemed to be expenses incidental to the discharge of the office. I find nothing about retroactivity to 1946 in the bill before me. In any case it would not be competent for the Ontario legislature to make a provision of that kind retroactive for federal income tax purposes.

It is regrettable that when a sound principle is given recognition, such recognition should be open to the complaint that it fails by reason of omission, especially when those omissions are discriminatory in their nature. My colleagues, the hon. members for Vancouver-Quadra and Lake Centre, have drawn attention to two flaws in the section, both of which it seems to me are in their nature omissions, and both of which are discriminatory in their effect.
I wish first of all to say a word about the point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, because I do not think the minister has answered it adequately. He

Income Tax Act
referred to the question of the position of elected members of school boards-or, for that matter, elected members of other boards forming part of any municipal government. The minister made the statement, as I understood him, that members of school boards, or school trustees, could always recover their expenses. Speaking of the board of education in the city of Toronto, which has under its charge the biggest municipal school system in this country, I wish as a former member of it to say now that his statement is not correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why can they not? Will not the school board pay them?
Expenses the trustees incur?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
No; there is no provision made for the payment of expenses of trustees.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is nothing to prevent the school board paying the actual out of pocket expenses of trustees, and the member of the school board does not have to include that in his income.
I can tell the minister that no provision is made for the payment of their expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is up to the school board.

It will be interesting to note what will happen in the light of the discussion here today. I can tell the minister that no provision is made for the payment of expenses to school trustees.
Why should a distinction be drawn between elected members of school boards and elected members of city councils? There is no distinction in principle. It is quite true, as the minister has said, that in many municipalities no provision whatever is made for the payment of any form of remuneration to members of school boards or boards of education. That is a matter for the provincial legislatures. But where provincial legislation does permit the payment of remuneration to school trustees or members of boards of education, whatever form the organization may take, I submit that there is no ground whatever that will warrant this discrimination, that will acknowledge the principle of permitting an exemption in a case of this kind for expenses incurred by an elected member of a municipal council and will deny similar exemption to an elected member of a board of education or, for that matter, any other elective office on a municipal board.
Then on the other point raised by the hon. member for Lake Centre, I wish to say that there is a straight case of discrimination. I submit that where it is clearly the

intention of the provincial legislature to permit municipal councils to pass bylaws or resolutions making retroactive the effect of provisions of the kind contemplated in this section, that determination should be acknowledged by the federal authorities and effect given to it. There is not much use passing legislation here which is pictured as being remedial in nature and retroactive if in fact it is going to be given such a meagre and narrow interpretation that even the intent of provincial legislatures with respect to it is to be ignored or even defeated.
Coming back to the point I made at the beginning, here is a sound principle which is recognized in the section. Why cannot we have an unimpaired recognition of the principle? Why must there be these gaps left in that recognition, especially when the result is discrimination?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister said earlier in this discussion that this legislation is based on the fact that there is legislation providing exemption from income tax for the expense allowances paid to members of the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To private members.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister is reminding us that it does not apply to him. Of course he gets in addition a motorcar allowance of $2,000 which is free from income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
More discrimination.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: As hon. members know, this was granted first to members of the House of Commons. Then it was extended to members of provincial legislatures. Now it is being extended to members of municipal councils. As all hon. members know, when some of our friends in the press gallery have nothing better to write about they write about the remuneration received by members of parliament. This is a subject that is frequently written about. In view of recent press rumours to the effect that some day there might be a change in the basis of remuneration for members of parliament, perhaps involving the elimination of any exemption from income tax; if that were done, what would be the minister's attitude toward these exemptions to elected officers in other jurisdictions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I must confess that I have not given it any thought up to the present time and would not want to give a snap answer. I think the whole situation would have to be looked at. Members of the committee will recall that the tax-free expense allowance provided to members of parliament was the

subject of some criticism. I felt that that was unwarranted. I happen to know why it was introduced by my predecessor, Mr. Ilsley.
It was introduced at a time when the income tax rates were just about double what they are now. In order to give members of parliament even a reasonable amount for the added expenses which they were incurring, if it were to be made fully taxable it would have meant raising the indemnity to more than double the $4,000 as it then was. So it was decided to use the method of granting a tax-free expense allowance.
If one were able to get the tax scale down to even more modest proportions than it has been possible to do at the present time I may say-I can only express my personal view-that I would not be unduly enamoured of tax-free expense allowances. When it is possible to do it, I think it is preferable to have the income all taxable and such expenses as are involved paid on an actual basis. That is only my personal opinion and I would not want to feel committed to it. It must depend on the circumstances existing at the time. As members of parliament we must recognize that our remuneration is tied in with the expense allowance.
Do I understand that the minister is not prepared to make a change?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not this year.

There are one or two comments I should like to make. It seems to me that the minister has not answered the criticism of discrimination. He has been less than convincing when he says that the phrase "paid by the municipal corporation" applied only to municipal officials and not to members of school boards. I wonder, with the discrimination and inequality that have been pointed out, if it would not be reasonable, in view of the fact that this has an impact on every municipality in the dominion, to ask the minister to reconsider it. It is not an overwhelmingly important point, but nevertheless it is of great importance. I really feel that the minister has not answered the criticism which has been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have tried to answer it but probably have not done so satisfactorily. I am not prepared to state that there is discrimination. My personal experience is that most municipalities do not pay their municipal officials. This work is done voluntarily as a public service. It is only in the larger municipalities where the practice has existed of paying the municipal officials. As I said before, it has always been open to any
Income Tax Act
municipal official to receive from the municipality any out of pocket expenses which he has incurred.
This special privilege of a tax-exempt lump sum allowance is being extended for the first time to elected municipal officials. I would want to know a good deal more about the organization of school boards of one kind and another across the country before I would want to extend this principle still further. I do not think I can add anything to what I have said already.

If a member of a school board is elected in exactly the same way as a member of a council, will he not then be eligible for the benefits of this section? I do not see how in fairness the department can get away from the wording "elected officer of an incorporated municipality." How is the department going to be able to step in and say that an alderman is an elected officer and that a member of a school board is not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the member of the school board is in law an elected officer of an incorporated municipality he would benefit from the section. In my province he would not because he would be a member of a completely separate corporation. Perhaps this would apply in British Columbia, but it would not in Quebec.
I think in British Columbia the member of the school board is elected in the same way as the member of the council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a matter of the legal interpretation of the section.

Mayors, reeves and members of municipal councils particularly in the province of Ontario, are probably the most overworked and underpaid people in public life in the whole country. I think this is an extremely good principle and absolutely justified. We must also remember that mayors and reeves of most municipalities have to fight an election every year, which I think is archaic in principle.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As I have indicated, I do not like the principle very much, any more than I like it for ourselves, but if we are going to do it for ourselves we may as well extend it to others.
Apparently this section is repeated in section 47.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is simply for the revised statutes. In effect half of the bill is a re-enactment of the amending provisions for the revised statutes. In all these taxing statutes we have to have a double enactment of the sections because, as my hon. friend knows, we are amending the new revised

Income Tax Act
statutes this year. Therefore the section to which he refers is really an enactment of this provision for the purpose of the revised statutes.
I read it rather rapidly. Is it in identically the same language?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It should be, with appropriate references, if necessary, to the revised statutes, but it is the same provision.

In subsection 2 it says that this section is applicable to the 1949 and subsequent taxation years. That is the part which is objectionable in my part of the country. The objection is along the lines that the hon. member mentioned a few minutes ago. In New Brunswick, and I think also in the other maritime provinces, there are a few elected school board members and to my knowledge they do not get any remuneration. Most of them are now appointed and are therefore out of the picture. But if you are going to permit officials of certain cities and towns in the dominion to go back and claim for 1946 I think it is discriminatory and unfair to us in those provinces that do not have that legislation. I feel that part should come out of the act, and I voice my objection to it because it is discriminatory so far as we are concerned. With respect to the future, that is a different matter. I agree with the principle.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot add anything to what
I	said to the hon. member for Lake Centre on that point.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 3-Employer's contribution to pension funds.

There is a point I should like to raise with respect to pension funds. I should like to urge on the minister that the time has come for some review of the whole position of pension funds in relation to section
II	of the Income Tax Act. The minister has received extensive representations this year with a view to broadening the provisions of section 11 of the act. I am sure there is nothing I can tell him on that subject that he does not already know. I have seen something of the briefs that have been submitted to him. The representations are along this line, that section 11 is much too limited in its scope at present and that the time has come when it should be extended to groups other than simply employees. There is a broad range of people in this country who are members of various kinds of groups who do not fall under the classification of employees, and no provision whatever is made for them at the present time in this law in relation to
TMr. Abbott.]
any pension plan that they as members of professional, labour or business associations may choose to set up.
Representations have come to the minister along this line proposing quite detailed provisions to deal with such cases. These representations come from responsible organizations and quite broadly representative associations. I know of one representation that was made to the minister on behalf of a group of such associations which included the following:	The Associated Dentists
Co-Operative, the Association of Professional Engineers of the Province of Ontario, the Canadian Dental Association, the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants, the Canadian Medical Association, the Certified Public Accountants Association of Ontario, the Commercial Travellers Association of Canada, the Daw Society of Upper Canada, the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada and the Toronto stock exchange.
There are ample safeguards that are possible. 1 know the minister has been somewhat concerned about trying to hedge any such extension of the scope of the legislation with ample safeguards. Many safeguards have been proposed, many of them of a quite practical nature which will in my view, after some study of the plans, adequately prevent any abuse of plans of this kind. There is comparable legislation in the United States congress. It seems to me without labouring the point-and, as I say, I am not speaking on it at length because the minister is already fully familiar with it-that effect should be given	to representations of this nature
and that the law should be amended to enlarge the present scope of section 11 so that organizations of the kind I have mentioned, including business associations as well as bona fide professional associations, would have the benefit of it.
Indeed, the scope of the proposed amendment would extend its benefits, according to the submission that has been made to the minister, in these words, to "bona fide agricultural, labour, business, industrial or professional associations, or similar organizations." I am aware that the minister has not said a final no to these representations and I am glad that he has given some indication that he is prepared to give the matter further consideration. For my part I should like to say that I hope as a result of further study a way may be opened up for amendment of section 11 at an early date that will enlarge the scope of its beneficial effects.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend most sincerely for raising this most important question because, as he has said, it is one that has been engaging the attention of myself and my

officials for a number of years. I decided that this year I should like, if the occasion offered, to make a considered and somewhat detailed statement as to the progress that we have made up to this time in considering this important question.
During the past year I have received, as my hon. friend has said, quite a number of requests from professional groups urging amendments to the Income Tax Act which would allow a deduction for income tax purposes similar to that now provided for employee contributions to approved pension plans. In effect, the substance of these requests is for tax postponement on savings devoted to the purchase of retirement annuities. This request, although supported by a wider group this year than ever before, is of course by no means new. It has been put forward each year, I think, over a considerable number of years and, as I say, a great deal of attention has been given to it both by myself and by officials of my department. But I have not yet been satisfied that I should recommend to the house this new departure in principle under the Income Tax Act. As I said at the outset, I welcome this opportunity to give the house some of the reasons for the position I have taken on the matter.
First of all I should like to explain how it comes about that employees are given a deduction for their contributions to approved pension plans. Some solution had to be found to the purely technical problem of preventing double tax on pension income. All would agree, I think, with the general rule that income should not be taxed both when it goes into the fund and again when it is paid out. A decision had to be made as to when such income should be taxed. As the committee will recall, following the Ives commission report some years ago we adopted the uniform system of taxing pension income when it is received as a pension out of the fund and freeing from tax, up to certain defined limits, income paid into the fund.
