Personally I think that was a wise decision, for the alternative would have meant taxing income when paid into the fund, that is, taxing the employee in a year on income which in fact he never received in that year, the employer having deducted the proper amount from his wage or salary and paid it directly into the pension fund. Likewise, the employee does not receive currently that which the employer contributes on his behalf into the fund. It would have been a still greater anomaly to have required the employee to include in his income for tax purposes this additional amount placed to his credit by the employer in the year in which he actually earned this benefit. These are
Income Tax Act
problems which were avoided by the principle of taxing only at the time the employee received his pension.
It is seen, therefore, that tax postponement for employees was introduced to solve the technical problem of removing double taxation and to avoid taxing employees on benefits earned in a year but in respect of which no cash equivalent was received in the year. I might now point out that neither of these problems exists in the case of the professional groups which have asked for tax postponement on savings; that is, their income is not now taxed twice and they are not taxed on income not actually received or receivable in the year. Accordingly, tax postponement granted to them would be a purely gratuitous measure of tax abatement not justified by the necessity of meeting technical problems in the taxing statute.
I think it is fair to say that, although the government is interested in seeing pension plans adopted in industry, the tax postponement feature did not arise out of a policy designed specifically to give positive benefits to taxpayers. Rather it was adopted to remove existing tax obstacles to the reasonable operation of pension plans. In view of these facts it is not very effective, it seems to me, to attempt to argue by analogy that, because employees have tax postponement as a solution to their particular problem, therefore self-employed persons should likewise have it in respect of their voluntary savings.
Much of the discussion of this subject alleges that the existing provisions discriminate unfairly against the self-employed who cannot participate in a pension plan. It might be suggested, I think, that this difference in the relative positions of the two groups can very easily be exaggerated. Some aspects are frequently overlooked. For example, those who devote their savings towards the purchase of endowment policies or annuities receive very reasonable tax treatment in that they are never taxed at all on the interest earned by the funds paid in right up to the date of maturity of the endowment or annuity contract. The employee in a pension plan, however, pays tax on all the interest earned on his payments into the fund right from the day of his first instalment payment. This, I suggest, is an extremely important difference in the two situations, and is one that is rarely recognized by those arguing for the benefits of pension plan legislation. Furthermore, in the case of the employee who put his savings into a pension plan, those savings are com-nletelv locked up and are not available to him in the ordinary course of events. The self-saver, on the other hand, always has his assets in a form available to him for emergency or for convenience. There is, of course,

Income Tax Act
no double taxation of funds used by the self-saver to purchase an endowment or annuity because the proceeds of their savings at maturity are tax free whether taken in a lump sum or in the form of an annuity. I suggest that an objective comparison of the relative positions of the two groups raises some question about accepting too readily the view that the self-employed are discriminated against.
Most of the requests which I have received for amendments to allow tax postponement on savings have come from well organized professional groups with national organizations. It seems clear, however, that once the law departed from its present principle of confining tax postponement to employees there would be no logical stopping point short of allowing this privilege to everybody, not merely to the self-employed but also to all employees who are not now covered by pension plans. The fact that certain groups have professional status with well recognized national organizations could not, I think, be regarded as a proper criterion for securing particular benefits under tax legislation. It is, therefore, on this basis of general applicability that I have had to consider this question of allowing tax postponement for savings.
The implications of such a move are extremely far-reaching. It is difficult to know what volume of savings would be attracted by this immediate monetary incentive, but I am inclined to think it would be extremely substantial. Most people, I think, would feel that they could not readily forgo immediate dollar savings of quite substantial proportions in their annual income tax bill if the proposal were adopted. It should be remembered that the funds devoted towards the purchase of retirement annuities would not necessarily have to come out of additional savings, as is the case where employees have contributions deducted from current wages and salaries. In the case of the self-employed person, who generally will have some other capital assets, he could secure the tax saving by merely changing the form of his assets. He could, for example, sell stocks and use the proceeds as an instalment payment on a retirement annuity. Again, it is not easy to estimate to what extent there would be a transformation in the form of capital assets now held by the ordinary citizen. However, whatever the volume of this switching of assets, it would be significant, I think, that under our tax structure monetary incentives would be offered for Canadians to invest their savings in a direction where the persons utilizing them would invest them almost entirely in debt or fixed interest bearing securities. I am not sure that at this stage of Canada's development I would like to take the responsibility

for directing the savings of the Canadian people away from equities into debt securities. To me this would be an ill-advised policy in a country where there is such an enormous demand for risk capital for the development of our country and where the opportunities for participating in the growth and development of our country are so important.
Now, Mr. Chairman, these are some of the reasons which have caused me to hesitate about accepting the representations which have been made to me on this question. As my hon. friend from Eglinton has pointed out, I do not regard myself as in a position to be dogmatic about the matter, but I do feel that the implications of allowing tax postponement which encourages savings in special directions are such as to warrant the most careful study. As I said at the outset of this statement, I have not felt that I wanted to take the responsibility for such a far-reaching move at this time.

I am sure the house appreciates that the minister in his statement has been as comprehensive as he has in the review of the problem. However, I may say that I am disappointed in the attitude it indicates, because I had hoped the minister was more open-minded on the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not taken a final position but the difficulties, the inequities, still appal me.

I did not say there were no problems attached to it, but the emphasis is laid on the problems and the minister minimizes the desirable objectives attached to it. The statement does leave me with some sense of disappointment and I wish to mention very briefly several of the points which the minister has made. I am not going to attempt a detailed refutation of all the points he has made-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I put them forward for consideration, as my hon. friend will appreciate.

Quite. In the first place, the minister has sought to distinguish the position of the employee because whatever is paid into the pension fund as his contribution does not come into his own hands in the form of income. I think that is not an accurate statement. It may well be that the money does not come into the hands of the employee and flow through those hands into the fund, but by arrangement with the employer the employee's pension contributions go directly from the employer into the pension fund. Surely that distinction is a matter of form only and not a matter of substance. There is no essential distinction in that regard between the case of an employee's contribution to a pension fund and that of a self-employed person.

Then there is the point made by the minister with regard to discrimination. I think, in the light of the discussion this afternoon, that I am just as allergic to any form of discrimination as the minister is, but, Mr. Chairman, if the principle is sound that the type of remedial legislation which I have been advocating should not be confined to members of bona fide associations or organizations, all right. Then let us have that wider recognition of the principle-but I do say that the principle is sound.
The reason this matter comes before the minister in the present form, namely a request on behalf of certain bona fide types of organizations, is that it was possible through such organizations to guarantee that there would not be abuses and to assure that the pension funds that would be established would be bona fide pension funds, that the contributions would be made into those funds and that the benefits would be such as were indicated by those responsible for the administration of the funds.
There is nothing unusual about that. That is part of the web and woof of the whole recognition in section 11 of the Income Tax Act of the pension fund; because it is not every pension fund existing today, even as between employer and employee, that is recognized for the purposes of section 11 by the minister. It is only those that are approved. This is not a question of discrimination at all. It was a question of guaranteeing the existence of such factors as will win the approval of the minister, just as you have provision made for approval by the minister under section 11(g) in the present act.
Let us consider further for just a moment the scope of the type of recognition that is being asked. It was proposed that it should be extended to bona fide agricultural, labour, business, industrial or professional associations or similar organizations. Let us take the case of a labour union today. If a labour union, within its own organization, decides to set up some form of pension or annuity scheme for its own members, their contributions thereto are not treated as exempt under section 11. Then let us take an agricultural organization. If a group of farmers in a bona fide organization decide to set up a pension plan, their personal contributions to that pension plan do not win any form of exemption under section 11 today. But the employee of an employer finds himself in a favoured position, notwithstanding what the minister had to say-which I think is a matter of form and by no means a matter of substance- because the contribution does not go into the hands of employees but goes direct from the employer into the pension fund. That is no basis of distinction in principle at all.
Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend wants to be fair. My real basis of distinction is why should one form of saving be singled out for tax postponement. That is the fundamental consideration.

That is the basis upon which the minister started his statement. I took the key struck by the minister in the opening part of his statement. I think there is no basis of distinction between the pension fund created by employer and employee on the one hand and the pension fund created by bona fide organizations on the other.
The recognition given by the act today, which the minister has defended in its limited terms, is confined to this particular situation, employer-employee pension funds-and not even all of those because they still must meet certain yardsticks laid down by the department before it will give its approval.
I do not wish to use the word "discriminatory" as applied to the present legislation. It is a very limited form of recognition of a principle that I think the government ought to encourage, namely the provision by people for their needs in the case of retirement. It is a very sound form of security that uses fiscal methods that are open to the minister in the form of the income tax to encourage people to provide for their old age, the days when after retirement they cease to be earning an income for their own support.
Here is a method at hand, it seems to me, not on the basis of discrimination but on the basis of the extension of a provision that has been recognized today and is fully established within the scope of the Income Tax Act. So far as I know, nobody has questioned the principle involved in section 11(f) and (g). It has never been questioned. It is accepted by everybody. It is fully established. If that principle is sound-and I think every member of this committee would say it is sound-I think there is no adequate answer to the plea that that sound principle now ought to be more widely extended.
I wish therefore to urge it again. I hope that the minister will see more merit in the proposal and fewer difficulties than he indicated in his comprehensive statement today, and that very soon we shall see an effort made, which will take the form of an amendment to this section, to give the kind of encouragement I have spoken of to pension funds established by bona fide agricultural, labour, business, industrial or professional associations or similar organizations.
I read earlier an enumeration of certain organizations who were parties to the submission of the brief to the minister. I want to make it quite clear to the committee that

Income Tax Act
they did not ask it for themselves alone. They were not seeking any discriminatory advantage for themselves. They were simply putting before the minister a case for the recognition, within this principle to which I have referred, of all organizations within the type of bona fide organizations to which I have referred. Let there be no thought in the mind of any hon. member that these organizations were seeking some selfish or discriminatory advantage.
Mr. Chairman, I submit that the principle Is sound and that it is worthy of extension. Many of these problems which the minister raised in his statement this afternoon it seems to me are capable of being dealt with by the application of the ingenuity that exists within the Department of Finance and the Department of National Revenue on the administrative side. They have overcome many other problems. This one is not free from difficulty, but I am convinced that, if there is a will here, a way will be found to overcome any administrative difficulties that the minister's statement may have conjured up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I just add a word here. I made my statement today in the hope that it would be subjected to close critical analysis not only by members of the House of Commons but by members of the legal and accounting professions and those who are as interested in this question as I am. I hope that it will be given that kind of analysis.

I just want to add a word. I am impressed by the difficulties outlined by the minister, but I share the feeling of the hon. member for Eglinton in the picture as he just presented it of this being purely a technical question by reason of the fact that the money did not go into the hands of the pensioners. That seems to me to be technical. The more substantial difficulty does seem to be that of distinguishing between the various kinds of funds.
The one point I wish to make is as to the reality of the problem. With the steeply graduated income tax we all know how difficult it is, even for people with substantial incomes, to save. When the minister spoke about the position of the class that we are talking about now, and mentioned their shares, their bonds and the difficulty of administration because of the changing about of those, may I say that after all that applies to only a small fraction of those we are talking about. We are really talking about people who, as things stand now, find it extremely difficult, as the hon. member for
[Mr. Fleming.)
Eglinton has said, to provide for their security, but who would like to do it notwithstanding the fact that the difficulties are great. I take it from the minister that he is pursuing the inquiry and that it is going to be earnestly pursued.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows they have a similar problem in the United States, because their system is somewhat similar, and they have not been able to solve it either. I have asked myself, if we are going to do that, why we should not allow the deduction of premiums on endowment policies and some of these other things. The thing is filled with complexity. I can assure the committee that it is far from one of those simple open and shut cases.

I think we should all approach this matter in the spirit in which the minister has left it; that is, he has given us a statement on which he is going to welcome suggestions and analysis. Perhaps it is a little premature to be suggesting that we are offering a detailed consideration of the matter, because we have not had the opportunity of studying it. I should like to ask the minister whether he himself will not give more consideration- to, and perhaps indeed a further elaboration of, the statement he made at the beginning or near the beginning of his presentation, that to extend the principle of tax postponement on payments into pension funds to those who are self-employed would be a new departure in principle.
I would ask him to consider that very carefully because it seems to me it is important to be clear as to whether it is in fact a departure in principle or merely an extension of an already established principle. The mere fact that money paid into a pension fund in the case of approved pension plans under an employer-employee arrangement is paid directly by the employer into the fund instead of going through the hands of the employee to me is not really a differentiation in principle from the -case where a selfemployed person receives the income and then pays into a pension or retirement fund which he is trying to set up for himself. The fact is, and I am sure the minister will not question this, nor anyone else, the portion of his wages which is paid on behalf of the employee into the pension fund is nevertheless wages.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

Surely no one would deny that it is wages; and if it were not for the provisions of section 11 it would be taxable income as wages or salary or earnings.

Well, now, in the case of a professional or a self-employed person-let us not confine it exclusively to the professions-a person who is carrying on a small contracting business is certainly not a professional man, but he is not very far removed from the status of an actual wage earner. He is in fact contributing to the development of the country, and he is providing employment for others. Yet just because he is self-employed, his payments into the pension plan or retirement plan which he is trying to build up for himself are not tax-postponed. I cannot see that there is any distinction in principle, because the moneys he pays into the fund form part of his general earnings at the beginning, and then are paid out by him. I cannot see any distinction in principle there from the fact that the moneys paid into an approved pension plan on behalf of the employee are in fact part of his wages, but instead of being paid by him are paid into the pension plan.
I think that is an important hurdle to overcome. That is why I think it is worth while doing some fairly close reasoning on it. I would ask the minister to do some more, because it seems to me if it could be agreed that this is not a departure in principle, as he suggests, but merely an extension of an already established principle, perhaps the first and most important hurdle would have been overcome.
As to one of the other difficulties raised by the minister himself, namely that to make this extension would perhaps open up very wide fields of conversion of savings into interest-bearing securities rather than into equity capital, I would ask the minister whether he does not think a practical solution and one not causing very great difficulty would be found by placing the same limitation on the amount that might be paid into selfemployed persons' pension funds as I understand is now placed on the amount of employees' earnings; that is, a ceiling on the amount that may be paid into the pension fund and thus on which the tax is postponed. Surely the difficulty seen by the minister and stated there would be very real if there were no limitation on the ceiling, so that all savings might eventually be channelled into a new form of investment. But if you placed a ceiling on it-and I believe all the plans that have been suggested do envisage a ceiling-it seems to me it cuts down that difficulty very considerably.
May I just add a word on that one point. It does seem to me hardly a valid objection for the minister to raise that difficulty in the way of making a tax exemption for payments
Income Tax Act
into pension funds by self-employed persons, when in fact he does not appear to view with alarm the present situation with respect to the investment of pension plan funds which are established for employees. In other words, the point I am trying to make is that the pension funds established under an employer-employee relation on which there is a tax exemption are invested now, as I understand it-certainly a great majority of them are- in interest-bearing securities. I should doubt very much whether any one of these approved plans would be open to investment in equity capital or common stocks. If the minister is prepared to contemplate that form of investment in interest-bearing securities, then why is he so horrified at the idea that this type of pension plan might also have its funds invested in non-equity capital? It seems that what is fair for one is fair for the other, and the difficulty is greatly diminished when you realize and place on the new proposal the same relative ceiling that now applies to the old one.
I want to express realization of the fact that there are difficulties, and that no one can ask the minister to make any sudden or snap decision. It is obvious that the matter has been considered by him most carefully for some time. Perhaps, however, one might be permitted to express here the hope that, as the minister himself has indicated, he may not be occupying the position he now holds for very much longer-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A little new blood would do no harm.
-he too will be concerned about leaving for himself a lasting monument in the affections of the Canadian people by taking at least one forward step along the lines that we are now urging.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

postponement. I tried to make clear in my statement that the discrimination against the self-saver is not as great as it might appear to be on the surface. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Those plans, as I recall it, are not plans where there is any pension element at all. It is merely, as my hon. friend said, profit sharing. But the shareholder does not get profits in cash. They are accumulated to his credit on the books of the company. Under those circumstances we have never given tax postponement for deferred profit sharing. I think that would be a real departure in principle which it would be difficult to justify in respect of other taxpayers. The plans are probably very desirable plans. On section 5-Amount received by broker to be included.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have some amendments. Perhaps before moving them I might give a brief explanation, unless some other hon. members would wish to speak first.
The actual form of the amendment is somewhat technical because two or three sections are involved, but what the section in the bill intended to accomplish was this: As the committee knows, brokers carry stocks in street names, and receive dividends on those stocks. They do not know at the time

to whom the dividends belong. They set them up in their books as liabilities. The section as contained in the act provided that they would have to pay tax on the dividends in the future, and the right to claim deduction-
What has happened in the past in this connection?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am told that in the past they have just been carried on the books, and in some cases have been taken into the incomes of the firms. The original proposal was that in future these dividends would have to be taken into the firms' incomes and be subject to tax, but that when paid out to the real or actual owners, deductions could be claimed.
We have now received representations from some of the leading members of the profession, and from officers of the stock exchange, in which they tell us that, in fact and in law, they do not consider these funds to be their funds. They carry them on their books as a type of trust fund, but they do not consider that they can ever go into their accounts as income to the firms or to the brokers.
They have been informed by their legal advisers that there is no statute of limitations applying with respect to these receipts, and that there is always a claim there. Under those circumstances the proposed amendments will provide that they will take the full amounts standing on their books as being income held for undisclosed principals. They will deduct 25 per cent as a withholding tax at the source. Then they will continue to hold the moneys to their credit in the books. When an undisclosed principal comes forward, if he ever does, and claims a payment of dividends accruing to his credit, he gets them and he takes credit for the 25 per cent which has been withheld at the source. And if by any chance his effective rate of tax were less than 25 per cent he would get a refund.
That is the plan being substituted for what is contained in the bill now before the committee. It seems to me that it meets the position taken by the recipients of these dividends, that they have never belonged to them. On the other hand it is clear that they are income belonging to someone. So it has seemed reasonable to provide for a withholding tax of 25 per cent, which the real owner can claim as a credit if and when he gets the dividends.
That is the way in which it will operate. As I say, that withholding tax will not be exigible until the 1954 period. And, if one may use a slang expression, if it should

develop that there are some bugs in this thing which we do not now see, there will be ample opportunity to correct the inequality. But the essential thing we are trying to do is to be fair in these matters, but at the same time to get a tax on what admittedly is income subject to tax.
That is the purpose. I have a number of amendments to move but, before doing so, I would be prepared to listen to any questions hon. members may have to ask.

May I suggest it might be better if we could see the amendments before we attempt to ask questions. The changes involved in the amendments, as outlined by the minister, will have to be considered carefully. It is now two minutes to five and, as no doubt we will proceed with the discussion of public and private bills at five o'clock, perhaps the minister would be prepared to let this section stand until this evening, so we could examine the amendments in the meantime.

I am aware of the difficulty which necessitated this section, and I am not going to quarrel with the method of solving the problem presented by the purchase of securities in the middle of the interest period, as proposed by the new section 19A. I would submit to the minister for that reason that the retroactive effect of this remedial legislation should not be confined to the year 1952 but should be extended further back. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Assuming that it is not possible to persuade the minister to make a further change in this matter at the present time, I rise to serve notice on him, or whoever may be minister of finance when he lays down that portfolio, that I for one intend to keep up the effort to get the floor under medical expenses allowed as deductions for income tax purposes wiped out altogether. Naturally we welcome the change that is being made in that the floor is being reduced from 4 per cent to 3 per cent. We welcome that change even as we welcomed the change back in 1944 when Mr. Ilsley saw fit to reduce the floor from the original 5 per cent to 4 per cent after considerable agitation on the floor of the House of Commons.
I still find it impossible to follow the argument of the Minister of Finance that there is anything sacred about what he calls the average of medical expenses, as though that average should provide a floor of this kind. When a Canadian taxpayer is hit with medical expenses-and when these expenses hit they

Income Tax Act
are usually quite substantial-it is no consolation to him to be told that the extra bills with which he is confronted are just the average, up to 3 per cent of his income. The plain fact of the matter is that when such expenses hit, particularly when they come unexpectedly, the average Canadian is not in a position to meet them. I think it is pretty generally held that it would be only fair to wipe out the floor altogether and grant medical expenses right from the first dollar as deductible for income tax purposes.
I should throw in the qualifying sentence that I do not disagree with the ceiling the minister has placed on this exemption, even as he has a ceiling on charitable donations, but to me there is no justification whatsoever for the present floor. I did not happen to be here at the time the budget debate was in process. It was unfortunate; but it so happened that because I was not able to be here, because I was back home, I was able to get right away the reaction of the man in the street to the budget as a whole and to its various items. I can tell the minister that there was a great deal of disappointment on the part of ordinary Canadians that he only reduced the floor from 4 per cent to 3 per cent instead of wiping it out altogether.
Canadians have not forgotten the fact that a year ago the House of Commons supported a motion which went as far as a private member's motion could go in asking that consideration be given .to the complete removal of the floor, and that the minister did not see fit to remove it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
I submit the newspapers of the country were not all wrong in the view they took as a result of the decision on that occasion. At any rate, even if the minister thinks he made a mistake, he helped to bring about the realization on the part of the Canadian people that here was a reform that was needed; here was an injustice that should be removed; and I am quite satisfied that it is held far and wide throughout Canada that there should be no floor of this kind at all. Our efforts across the years

have paid dividends to some extent in that we have had this floor reduced, first from 5 per cent to 4 per cent, and now from 4 per cent to 3 per cent. I can tell the minister that we shall keep up our efforts. I hope that in another year it will be wiped out altogether, and that it will be recognized that medical expenses right from the first dollar up to the ceiling set under the act should be allowed as deductible for income tax purposes.
I would like to ask the minister how this works out. Does it apply at all to 1952, where medical expenses were incurred in 1952 but not paid until 1953?

This is a very technical amendment. The committee may recall that two or three years ago when we introduced the system of permitting 15 per cent tax to be paid on undistributed surpluses, we put in what might be colloquially described as a block. We did not allow surpluses in controlled companies to be gotten out through reorganization in a way that would in fact provide an evasion of the intention of the act. The block was a pretty rigid one, and it was found that in a certain number of cases a perfectly legitimate reorganization of the corporate structure between parent and subsidiary was prevented by this rigid block.
This section has been worked out by the officials of my department after a study of circumstances in particular cases in order to remove those inequities. I have been assured, and I am satisfied myself, that it does remove the discrimination which existed with respect to those particular concerns of which there are a fairly limited number.

Here again I must ask the indulgence of the committee. This is a new section which relates to benefits to employees as the result of stock option agreements. It has been given a great deal of attention since the provision was first put in, and I should like to make the following statement before asking one of my colleagues to move an amendment.
During the last week or so since the bill received first reading I have had numerous representations regarding this clause in the bill which is designed to take care of a loophole which now exists in our law with respect to stock option plans. While the provisions of the clause now before us were designed to cover the relatively narrow field of stock option plans, the proposed legislation does bring into perspective the more general problem of how to treat the more usual type of employee stock purchase plan as distinct from stock option.
The amendment which I am going to ask one of my colleagues to move deals with the
[The Chairman.)
two subjects under one general provision. Where, under the existing law, benefits to employees under the ordinary stock purchase plans were potentially taxable under section 5 (1) (a) of the act, the amendment here proposed introduces a specific taxing provision for these benefits. The benefit to be taxed under both the stock purchase plans and the stock option plans is the difference between the purchase price of the share to the employee and its value at the time he acquired it. This benefit need not be included along with other income for tax purposes and thus put the employee in a higher tax bracket than would otherwise be the case. It will be open to him to have the benefit treated as a lump sum and taxed at a rate determined by the relationship between tax and income of his three previous years. The amount so determined will be reduced by 20 per cent of the benefit.
I might explain why this 20 per cent abatement against tax appeared to be a reasonable degree of relief. Section 5 of the law, while defining generally the scope of the tax on wages and salaries, provides that certain of what I might call fringe benefits need not be included in income. For example, the benefits obtained under group insurance plans need not be included in income. Neither is the employee required to include in his income the dollar value of his benefits under medical service plans. These facts suggest that it would not be unreasonable to exclude by some device moderate benefits received under stock purchase plans, for example.
A further point in this connection is that although the benefits received by the employee under stock purchase or stock option plans are regarded as income from office or employment, that is, it is regarded as remuneration, the corporation providing remuneration in this form to its employees does not charge it against its profit and loss account for purposes of corporation income tax. Thus it might be said that we are getting corporate income tax in a larger amount because the corporation decides to benefit its employees in this way.
These facts suggested that a degree of abatement equal to the low bracket of corporate tax might be a reasonable measure of relief to adopt. Accordingly, as I stated above, the tax as calculated on the effective average rate for a three year period will be reduced by 20 per cent, which is the minimum rate of tax on corporations.
I should add that it was not the intention in introducing this legislation to interfere with normal employee stock purchase plans which

have been introduced by a number of corporations, but it was felt that it was necessary to prevent an abuse of these stock option devices through allowing employees, perhaps executives of a corporation, to get very large benefits which would not be taxable.
I would ask that my colleague, the Minister of Public Works, move another long and very carefully drafted amendment which gives effect to the policy I have just enunciated and, as well, the corresponding amendment for part II.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the bill to be founded on this resolution is to consolidate, revise and modernize the legislation governing pensions and retirement allowances for members of the public service of Canada.
The first provision of this sort was enacted by parliament in 1870. In succeeding years there were numerous changes and revisions.
10,	1953
Public Service Superannuation Act Broadly speaking, the present pattern of contributory superannuation benefits was established under the Civil Service Superannuation Act of 1924.
In the nearly 30 years that have elapsed since then the 1924 act has been amended by parliament on ten separate occasions. The present legislation thus consists of the 1924 act plus ten amending acts. Moreover, there has been a great deal of experience gained in the administration of our act, and there has also been a steady and continuous development of pension policies and practices in private industry and in government employment, both in this and in other countries. There is, therefore, a very strong case for consolidation, revision and modernization at this time.
This will be a rather lengthy and technical bill. In making a statement at this resolution stage I propose to limit myself to an explanation of the important new principles which have been incorporated in the bill.
The first important new principle is that in future the benefits under the plan will be a matter of right rather than a matter of grace. Hitherto all payments of superannuation and related benefits have, as a matter of law, been grants by the governor in council *-rewards for good and faithful service. Even pensions to widows under the present law are dependent upon their "worthiness" to receive them. The new bill will depart from this somewhat archaic concept, and will establish the benefits clearly as a matter of right.
A second principle, which is closely related to the first, is that the bill will go just as far as is practicable in incorporating in the act itself all the rules governing contribution, calculation of length of service and benefits. The old act, based on a concept of grants and awards, naturally and perhaps inevitably gave very broad regulation-making powers to the governor in council and required that every award should be approved by the governor in council. Some regulation-making power, some element of discretion must be given to the governor in council, because the human factors and circumstances are so varied that it is quite impossible to cover every possible combination in an act of parliament. But when the bill receives first reading hon. members will find that it covers a much wider field in much greater detail, and that the regulationmaking power, while requiring a somewhat lengthy description, is restricted to dealing with exceptional and unusual cases or combinations of circumstances, and with that
3728	HOUSE OF
Public Service Superannuation Act degree of discretion which must be given if genuine hardships and practical injustices are to be avoided.
A third new principle, and the one which will have the greatest practical and beneficial results, is the proposal to extend the coverage of the plan to the great majority of all regular full-time public servants. Broadly speaking, the old act covers only those government employees of so-called permanent status. I estimate that the new bill will bring at least an additional 60,000 employees under the act; that is, it will probably almost double the number of employees covered by the plan. Our proposal is that in so far as it is practicable every regular full-time government employee will begin to build up superannuation rights from the commencement of his employment. The bill will not cover, of course, casual or part-time employees, nor is it possible at this time to apply it to the majority of prevailing rates or seasonal employees. But with these and a few other exceptions the intention is to provide a scheme of the broadest possible coverage.
The new bill will provide improved benefits in certain and rather limited sets of circumstances. The rates of contribution will be evened out to a straight 5 per cent for women and 6 per cent for men. The improvements in benefits are not major in character but are designed to smooth out the pattern of benefits and to remove some anomalies. Care has been taken to keep the fund actuarially sound, on the basic principle that the employees' contributions, plus an equal amount contributed by the employer, that is, the government, plus the accumulating interest on the total fund, shall be fully adequate to meet the calculated liabilities of the fund.
As I said earlier, this will be a rather lengthy and technical bill. I am sure hon. members will not want to have two overlapping debates. It seems to me that the appropriate time for a useful general debate will be on the second reading of the bill when its text will be before us. When I come to move second reading I shall be able to give some further information and explanations, but even then I shall not attempt to cover details or go into purely technical points. I suggest that the most effective way to deal with this bill in all its detail will be to refer it to the banking and commerce committee for study and report, and as soon as the bill has received second reading I shall so move.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am particularly pleased that this resolution has come forward. I have been one who has been rather appreciative of the civil service superannuation legislation. Canadians generally can be very pleased with the superannuation provisions for the public service and that they compare favourably with those in other jurisdictions. Indeed I hold the view that they are the best of any of which I am aware in any jurisdiction.
I have always felt there was not sufficient appreciation of the splendid work done on this subject by the committee in 1923 under the chairmanship of the late Hon. James Malcolm. The report of that committee was the basis for the present superannuation legislation, and the 1924 act was based upon it.
Then in 1944 there was an amendment which could be considered quite important in that for the first time it removed the discrimination against permanent civil servants who were paid other than by a stated annual salary. It opened up the right of great numbers of long-term civil servants to come under the act. Prior to 1944 not only was it necessary that a civil servant, before coming under the act, must be permanent, but also that he be paid a stated annual salary. That had the effect, of course, of excluding employees in the printing bureau where the pay was on a weekly salary basis similar to that in the printing trades. It also excluded prevailing rate employees who were paid on an hourly or daily basis. Again in 1947 there were further substantial changes liberalizing the act.
As I interpret the words of the minister, this bill will have the effect of permitting all long-term employees in the service to

come under the provisions of the superannuation act. An unfortunate terminology is used in connection with civil service matters in that some employees are classed as permanent while others are classed as temporary, although the latter may have been employed for a great number of years. The use of those terms has had a most unfortunate effect in discriminating against some longterm employees. It denies that peace of mind and comfortable assurance as to the future which in itself contributes so much to the efficiency of the service that is given in this way. In a very large measure the continuing business of this country under one government and another depends upon a high standard of civil service and upon that feeling of assurance that is given by legislation which avoids any feeling of unfairness or unjustness.
Canadians have every reason to be proud of the standard of our civil service. The members of this government, and of every government, should at all times be careful to preserve the great traditions of that civil service. The minister stated this evening that this legislation is going to reform the Civil Service Superannuation Act. Quite a few reforms are needed. One of them which has not been mentioned tonight is the compulsory retirement age of civil servants. If my understanding of the legislation is correct, civil servants have the option today of retiring at 60 and are forced to retire at age 65. In view of the increased life expectancy in recent years that compulsory age of 65 is outmoded. It is wrong, and it is financially dangerous to the country.
When we pick up our newspapers today we find that it is very difficult to get help in Canada. I came back from the west the day before yesterday, and I picked up the Toronto Star. I found in that paper page after page of help wanted ads. Farmers, chemists, bookkeepers, machinists and others were wanted. There were eight pages of help wanted ads in that particular paper, and the same is true of every paper from Newfoundland to British Columbia today. You just cannot hire people in Canada. That being so, is it sensible to force our civil servants to retire at the age of 65 if they do not wish to? I personally do not think it is. I was reading an article in a United States magazine not long ago which said that the chief of the United States public health service, when speaking on this question of forced retirement at the age of 65, said that it is costing the United States every year 1,250,000 workers who would earn $4 billion. If these figures are correct, and if Canadian figures are somewhat similar, I suppose it must be costing us across the country, industry and government, at least 150,000 workers, and perhaps a national production of about $400 million a year.
Time and again the government has suggested to private industry that it would be well advised to keep its employees beyond the age of 65. It seems sensible to me to suggest that the government should give industry an example. When this legislation is being reviewed the government should consider extending the compulsory age of retirement of civil servants from 65 to at least 68. There are a good many civil servants who would welcome a reform of that nature, because they find it very difficult to retire with the cost of living as high as it is. Another aspect is that when a man retires he usually deteriorates physically and mentally. That kind of reform would also save the taxpayer a good deal of money.
Today the taxpayer is being forced to pay a large share of the retirement pensions of civil servants rendered non-productive usually against their own desires. When this matter goes to the committee I hope the government will give consideration to the reform I have suggested.

I shall be happy to do that. I am afraid I have not the number of civil servants under the act at the moment. That is readily available and I can get it in a few minutes. In any event I can do it on second reading.
I had not intended to make a statement at the committee stage about this particular problem of those civil servants who were in the old department of soldiers' civil re-establishment, but we have a few minutes before ten o'clock and it may be helpful to consider it. It is a matter which can be discussed in committee, but in its consideration it might be helpful if I were to outline the facts in connection with these particular civil servants.
When the Civil Service Superannuation Act was passed in 1924 it was provided that those who were permanent civil servants within the meaning of the act on July 19, 1924, should be given the advantage of the average salary over the last five years of their service in the calculation of any allowances which might be granted to them. On the other hand any temporary employee on that date, or anyone else who subsequently became a permanent civil servant, was to be subject
10, 1953
Public Service Superannuation Act to a ten-year average salary provision instead of five years.
While ten years was determined in 1924 as a necessary factor for actuarial reasons in the benefit formula for future contributors, the five-year provision was put in primarily for the benefit of those who would be retiring shortly after 1924, after having gone through a recent period of low salaries which were supplemented by a cost of living bonus. The use of the five-year period instead of ten would be some compensation to that group, those who it was expected would be retiring very shortly after 1924.
The question which has now been raised concerns the department of soldiers' civil reestablishment employees appointed prior to July 19, 1924, when the superannuation act came into force. Prior to that date, the department of soldiers' civil re-establishment act provided that the minister, under regulations, might employ "such technical and special temporary staff as may be required . . ." It was also provided that the regulations should contain provision for the issue of certificates by the civil service commission in respect of the positions.
An amendment to the department of soldiers' civil re-establishment act which came into force on July 19, 1924, altered the power of appointment by removing the reference to temporary staff and at the same time expressly exempted the positions and staff from the operation of the Civil Service Act. The amending statute was expressed to have force and effect from November 10, 1919. The effect of this would be to exclude the positions and staff from the operation of the Civil Service Act as of that date and, as the deputy minister of justice expressed in an opinion of October 13, 1924, made it possible to give permanent status to employees of the department by regulation with retroactive effect to that date.
Prior to giving this opinion, however, the deputy minister of justice on September 24, 1924, expressed the opinion that all appointments made under the department of soldiers' civil re-establishment act prior to the amendment in 1924 were temporary only, there being no power in the minister to make a permanent appointment under the terms of the original act. The opinion of Mr. Edwards, who was deputy minister of justice at the time, continues:
I am of the opinion, in view of the terms of the statute, that such employees have only a temporary and not a permanent status. It follows that they are not eligible to become contributors under the new superannuation act.
In the light of the amendment and the opinion of the deputy minister of justice on

Public Service Superannuation Act October 13, 1924, a proposed regulation was considered by the treasury board in February, 1925; but the board on looking into the circumstances did not approve it.
When the Civil Service Superannuation Act was amended in 1927 the case ot these and others who had been excluded in one way or another was again raised. In speaking of these groups in general the then minister of finance stated that the act was not intended to include any employees whose sudden withdrawal from the service would impose unexpected demands on the fund. These demands would arise from the abolition of office provision which at that time carried with it the benefit of the grant of an allowance for life on the same basis as if the person concerned had retired because of age. The government therefore was not satisfied that the positions in this department were permanent and the employees therefore could not become contributors to the superannuation account.
Of course all the employees of the department would not necessarily have become permanent had the treasury board approved the regulation proposed in 1925. The department, however, hoped until 1927 to have the position altered, and on its own deducted amounts equivalent to the contributions which those of its employees who might have become permanent would have made to the superannuation account. The department forwarded these deductions to the superannuation branch of the Department of Finance. This branch, acting on the opinion of the deputy minister of justice of September 24, 1924, did not accept these payments but consistently returned them to the department. The department held them in a trust fund until 1927, and then returned them to the employees.
The employees of the department were, with some exceptions, blanketed in in 1929 under the department of pensions and national health act. Thereupon under the provisions of the act they were deemed to be permanent and were dealt with properly under part I of the superannuation act.
While it is true that these civil servants will not obtain the same advantages in the way of pension benefits as those who were permanent employees within the meaning of the act at that time, yet they are in the same position as that of any one of the 14,000 temporary employees in 1924 who may now be still employed.
Since that time thousands of decisions have been taken, allowances granted, and payments made on the basis of the decision of the treasury board in 1925 and, in effect, the


confirmation of parliament in 1927. To try to undo all this would lead to a hopeless tangle, and to grant special privileges now to those who are still employed would be absolutely unfair to those in a similar position who may have retired or to the widows of those who have died.
Any decision as to whether an employee should be regarded as permanent or not has to be made on the basis of the situation at the time the decision is made. Many functions and services of a department of government are not obviously of a permanent nature until a number of years have elapsed; and until that is accepted as evident the persons filling those positions have not been able to enjoy the privileges attached to permanency. That was the position of the department of soldiers' civil re-establishment up to 1929 when, as I say, it was blanketed in with the department of pensions and national health.
Happily, of course, we are taking steps to get away from any repetition of such an admittedly unsatisfactory situation, under the bill which is to be based upon this resolution. The old distinction between permanent and temporary is being removed, as well as the special abolition of office allowance, the existence of which made that former distinction necessary.
As I say, these questions can be discussed properly in the committee on banking and commerce, when officials of the superannuation branch and of my own department will be available to give any explanation which may be required. I propose to make a considerably more detailed statement on the motion for second reading, when I shall deal with the various provisions of the measure. However, it may be useful to have this factual statement on record tonight with respect to these employees of the old department of soldiers' civil re-establishment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I should like to ask the government leader when it is intended to bring in the estimates of the Department of National Defence.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I expect the return of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) over the week end; but my thought was that on Tuesday we would move to go into committee of supply at eleven o'clock and I would call three departments, which would be allowed to stand. Then we would take up the estimates of the Department of National Defence all day Tuesday and all day Wednesday. I do not know if we can go any further because I understand that three ministers are to leave during that week end to attend NATO meetings in Paris. That is what I was thinking at the moment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That was my reason for asking the question. I understand that the Minister of National Defence is to leave at the end of next week. There is no single department of
Business of the House
government that calls for such attention as does the Department of National Defence. We all recognize that under that one department half of all the money to be taken from the taxpayers during the current fiscal year will be voted. That department should be dealt with in a manner that recognizes the amount of taxation involved and the importance of the questions and answers that will be asked and given. I think I must express my own opinion that there is nothing more important for the Minister of National Defence than to be here for a continuous examination of the estimates of his department.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have given the only answer I can at this time. On Tuesday we shall move to go into supply but if there are speeches on agriculture all day I will be in a bad fix to get into national defence. I ask hon. members for their co-operation to let me get into supply on that day. I might wait until Thursday, but that would be late in the week. That is why I propose to move on Tuesday.
As to the importance of the department, everybody agrees with the Leader of the Opposition, but I have noticed that discussion does not always go according to importance. I took three days for just a small fraction of the amount to be spent on national defence.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is exactly the point. Can the minister inform us as to when the Minister of National Defence will be returning?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He will be away for a week, I think.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I gave that information without being sure. I shall have to consult my colleagues before giving a definite answer. The Leader of the Opposition may rely on my willingness to be co-operative and to help.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I can only say that the skill and dexterity with which the minister handled his own estimates is still apparent in his discussion of this subject. I understand from him that after the motion to go into supply on Tuesday is dealt with it is the intention to call the Department of National Defence?

And go as far as
possible.

March 12, 1953.
John A. Stevenson, Esquire,
Editor,
Saturday Night,
Toronto, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Stevenson:
In your column entitled "Ottawa Letter" in Saturday Night of March 14, you make the following statement:
"In the sessions of the select committee^ on defence expenditures, the persistent efforts of its chairman, Mr. Croll, and his henchmen to smother damaging evidence of governmental waste and mismanagement have not availed to prevent the opposition members from unearthing some very damning material to sustain their case. They are now licking their chops over some candid reports by important officials, and their severity can be gauged by the following two quotations:
'However, I could not fail to be impressed by the fact that for such a tremendous administrative machine there appears to be very little fighting strength', and 'a high percentage of the construction and other contracts were awarded on a cost plus basis, which the department itself has declared to be wasteful, inefficient, and an incentive to extravagance. *
It is very distressing when reputable journalists mislead the public, either through distortion or failure to take the trouble to ascertain the facts.
In your first quotation you may have some special knowledge not in my possession, but to describe the author of these remarks as "an important official" is stretching the truth beyond the breaking point.
With regard to the second quotation, its author is Arthur Blakely of the Montreal Gazette, writing in -that paper under date of
February 27. So far as I am aware, the government has not, as yet, appointed Mr. Blakely to any important office.
Yours sincerely,
C. M. DRURY, Deputy Minister

Ottawa, March 18, 1953.
Dear Mr. Drury,
You are the latest of a line of individuals ranging downwards from the late Lord Bennett and the late Mr. Mackenzie King, who have been "distressed" by my writings and I can only regard your distress over my reputation as a piece of childish condescension.
In respect to such strictures upon my work as yours I have always followed the maxim adopted by Disraeli in his dealings with women-"Never complain, never explain". But I will depart from it to the extent of referring you to the story written by Mr. Richard Jackson in the Ottawa Journal of March 16th and the admissions of the Prime Minister on the same day, which seem a complete answer to your charges about distortion and misleading the public.
I propose to ask the editor of Toronto Saturday Night to publish this correspondence between us.
I am,
Yours faithfully,
